title: High-resolution mapping of goose barnacle cover using multispectral drone imagery and LiDAR topography
content:
Abstract
Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) surveys can provide high-resolution remote sensing data to map small-scale fisheries, such as those targeting the goose barnacle Pollicipes pollicipes. We assessed the capability of multispectral imagery and Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) derived topography from drone flights to classify populations of P. pollicipes in north-western Spain. Two exposed rocky shores were surveyed using three drone flights equipped with a 10-band visible-near infrared (VNIR) and LiDAR sensors. These surveys produced orthomosaics and digital surface models with a spatial resolution of 7–9 mm. A supervised pixel-based Random Forest classifier was trained with a dataset composed of slope, northness, topographic ruggedness index (TRI), topographic position index (TPI), standardized reflectance, normalized green-red index, and area under the spectra between 531 and 668 nm. The capacity of the model to classify goose barnacles was validated with independent observations derived from the RGB photogrammetry, showing a global accuracy of 0.75, kappa of 0.50, F1 of 0.70, and a positive predictive value of 0.78. The most important predictors for the goose barnacle class were TRI, northness (a site-specific proxy of exposure to the dominant wave fetch), and slope. Topography showed elevated importance for classification of barnacles and mussels, proving the usefulness of high-resolution digital surface models for remote sensing of intertidal invertebrates. The cover (%) of goose barnacles in 50 × 50 cm cells was calculated from classification maps and the biomass was estimated using a biomass-cover model. Mean Goose barnacle cover ranged from 22% to 25%, while median cover ranged from 8% to 15%. Estimated biomass ranged from 5.0 to 5.7 (± 0.7) kg m−2 and was predicted using a cover-to-biomass relationship developed at nearby location, which explained 74.5% of the deviance. Biomass estimates were consistent with values of in situ sampling in previous studies carried out in Spain and Portugal. Our findings provide evidence of the relevance of topography for P. pollicipes remote mapping and highlight the potentiality of UAV topographic surveys for monitoring and managing small-scale fisheries. Replication of the proposed methodology across additional sites is recommended to improve model generalization.
